title: Permissions in a CRM
metaTitle: Permissions in a CRM, shown plainly
excerpt: Show a salesperson what they can change, and why a control is unavailable. A hidden button feels like a bug when they are between calls.
alt: An open notebook with the word Notes underlined, a fountain pen, and glasses on a wooden desk, the page left visible rather than shut.
caption: An open notebook on a desk, the page left where someone can read it. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a CRM hide buttons a person cannot use?
faqs.answer: No. A hidden button feels like a bug, especially to a salesperson between calls who remembers seeing the control yesterday. Show the action, mark it unavailable, and say why in one sentence. Hide it only when the person should not even know the action exists, which is rarer than teams think.

faqs.question: What should the explanation say?
faqs.answer: Say what they can do, and name the rule in their language. 'You can edit the note. Only the account owner can change the company name' is enough. Do not quote a role matrix, and do not tell them to contact an administrator without saying what the administrator can unlock.

faqs.question: How should permissions relate to errors?
faqs.answer: A permission is not a failed save. Explain it before they tap, so they never hit an error for a thing they were never allowed to do. If they reach a forbidden action from an old link, use the same explanation, and keep any text they typed.

markdown:
CRM permissions UX means showing the salesperson what they can do, and why something is unavailable. The person updating a record between calls will treat a missing button as a bug. They saw it last week, or a colleague described it, or the demo had it. Hidden controls waste the gap you designed the first screen to protect.

Say the boundary in the interface. Do not make them discover it by failing.

## Hidden buttons feel like bugs

A bug is something that should work and does not. A permission is a rule. When you hide the control, you erase the difference, and the salesperson files the rule as a defect. Support then explains the role. The explanation arrives after the note, which is late, and it arrives in a ticket, which is the wrong room.

Show the control in its unavailable state, next to the reason. Disabled, with a sentence, not a ghost that might be a loading glitch. "Change owner" can sit there, quiet, with "Only an admin can move an account." The rep stops hunting. They do the thing they are allowed to do, which is the note, and they understand the shape of the tool a little better. That understanding is what stops the same ticket next week.

There are exceptions. A control that reveals someone else's compensation, or a destructive admin action that would be dangerous to advertise to every rep, can stay out of the layout. The test is whether a reasonable person in this role would expect to see it because it is part of their job. Stage changes, notes, and reassignment inside their own book are expected. Payroll is not. Hide payroll. Explain the stage.

[The WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) frames quality as perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust, for web applications as well as pages. A control that is only conveyed by its absence is easy to miss and hard to understand. A control that is present, unavailable, and described in text can be operated up to the real boundary and no further. Color alone cannot carry "you cannot." The sentence has to be there for anyone who does not see the gray the way you intended.

## What they can do between calls

Lead with permission, not with prohibition. The first screen already has a verb. If they can log the call, that verb is live, and the sentence about the locked field is secondary. If they cannot log the call on this record, you have the wrong record on screen, or the wrong person, and the primary message has to be the way back to a record they can edit.

Typical boundaries, in language worth writing down:

1. They can add a note and a next step on their own deals.
2. They can edit the contact they just spoke to, not the legal entity's billing name.
3. They cannot delete the account, and they should see that deletion is an admin act, not a missing icon.
4. They cannot change an amount finance has locked, and the amount should still be visible so they do not think the deal vanished.

Write these as interface sentences, not as a policy PDF. The PDF will not be open between calls. The tooltip that disappears, and the title attribute that some browsers never really offered as a design, are almost as weak. Put the reason where the eye already is, beside the field.

Do not make them open a "why is this locked" dialog to learn a single clause. Dialogs are a context switch. The clause fits on the record. Use a dialog only when the reason is a real choice, such as requesting access, and even then the first line of the record should already have said they need to request it.

## Roles without a matrix lecture

The product has roles. The screen should not teach the matrix. "Owner," "admin," and "finance" are enough vocabulary if they match how the company talks. A custom role named "CRM_EDITOR_TIER_2" is a database key that escaped. Map it to a noun a rep would use, or stop showing the key.

If the reason depends on a person, name the role, and name the person when that is helpful and not a privacy problem. "Ask Sam, the account owner" is actionable. "Ask an administrator" is a corridor. On a small team the owner is known. On a large team, "account owner" plus the ability to copy their name is the compromise. Do not build a ticketing flow inside the CRM for a one-line rule unless the organization truly requires a request. Most of the time the rep needs to proceed with the note and mention the locked field to Sam later. Let that be easy.

Avoid permission theater: a lock icon on every field, including the ones they can edit, "for consistency." Icons without a difference stop meaning anything. Lock the locked ones. Leave the editable ones looking editable. The contrast is the lesson.

Temporary access, like covering a colleague's book for a week, should look temporary. "You can edit Northwind until Friday, while Sam is out." Otherwise they will be confused on Monday when the field locks, and they will call it a regression. The product changed nothing except the truth. Say the truth in advance.

## The dangerous actions

Delete, merge, export of the whole book, and bulk reassignment are not between-call actions. They can be visible to the people who hold them, and they should be hard to hit by accident. A confirmation that names the object is the minimum. "Delete Northwind and its 40 notes" is a confirmation. "Are you sure?" is not, because by the time someone is sure they are often sure about the wrong record.

For everyone else, these actions are the explained absences, not secret buttons that appear if you know a URL. If an old link still hits the endpoint, the response has to be the same sentence, not a raw forbidden page and not a half-applied delete. Security that depends on hiding the button and hoping is not the design. The server enforces the rule. The interface admits the rule. Both are required. A handsome disabled button that the API still honors is a costume.

Merging duplicates is the dangerous action reps actually need. They hit a duplicate between calls more often than they hit delete. Give them a safe version: "These two people share an email. You can suggest a merge." Suggestion is not the merge. The owner confirms. The rep's note still saves on the record they chose. Do not block the note on a data-cleaning project.

## A second login in the test

Test permissions with two real roles, not with a superuser who has never seen a disabled field. Sit a rep account next to an admin account. Open the same deal. The rep should be able to say, without help, what they can change and why the rest is quiet. The admin should recognize the same screen, with more verbs, not a different product.

Read the disabled reasons with a screen reader. If the only signal is a color and a mouse tooltip, the boundary is invisible to some of the people who depend on the record. Put the reason in text that is always available. WCAG's principles are the reminder: if it cannot be perceived and understood, it is not explained, however obvious it looked in the mock.

Also test the expired permission in the middle of a note. Sam removes them from the account while they are typing. On save, keep the draft, explain the new boundary, and offer the closest legal action, which might be sending the note to Sam rather than attaching it. Dumping them to a generic forbidden page is the bug they will remember.

## Do not encode the org chart in the pixels

Permissions change. Reorgs happen. If every screen was designed around today's three roles, the next role will be a pile of exceptions. Design the pattern once: a verb is either available, or it is visible with a reason. The reason is a short string the policy can fill. The layout does not change. What changes is which verbs are live.

That pattern belongs in the component, reviewed like any other component. Designers should not redraw disabled states as one-off tooltips on each page. Engineers should not invent a second pattern in settings. One treatment, used on the record, on search results, and on the bulk bar. Inconsistency is how "hidden" creeps back in, because a new page forgot the sentence and someone said "just don't show it."

Document the pattern in the same place you document buttons, in Figma and in the code. Hanabi's builds keep that kind of decision in the interface system so the next screen does not freelance. A CRM will have dozens of records. The permission sentence should feel identical on all of them, the way the save verb does.

## What the rep tells a colleague

The best test is the sentence they repeat. After a week, a good permission model produces a sentence like "I can note it, I can't rename the company." A bad one produces "the button is gone, try logging in as Sarah." You want the first sentence. It means the product taught the rule at the moment of work, and Sarah can stay on her own calls.

Listen for the second sentence in support tags and in the gaps between meetings. If you hear it, stop adding roles and fix the explanation. More roles on top of hidden buttons multiply the folklore.

Search is where a locked record often gets discovered, because the rep could not see it in their list and went looking. [Search inside a CRM](/blog/search-inside-a-crm) is the next piece, because when navigation fails they will search, and the results have to be in their language, with a way back to the record they left.
